title: Vector Space
body:
A **vector space** is a set on which you can add elements and multiply by scalars, such that
those operations behave the way they do for arrows in the plane. That is the whole idea: take
[[Vector]] arithmetic, forget where it came from, and keep only the rules. Anything obeying the
rules is then entitled to every theorem in the subject.

This is the same move [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] makes with a [[Group]]: name the operations, list the
axioms, and inherit the results. A vector space is a richer structure than a group (two
operations rather than one, plus a field of scalars underneath), but the reason for defining it
is identical. That underneath part is literal: a vector space is defined **over a [[Field]]**, and
it has to be a field rather than a [[Ring]] because the axioms and row reduction both need to
divide by a scalar.

## The axioms

For a set $V$ with addition and scalar multiplication over $\mathbb{R}$, and any
$\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w} \in V$ and scalars $c,d$:

| Addition | Scalar multiplication |
|---|---|
| closed: $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in V$ | closed: $c\mathbf{u} \in V$ |
| commutative: $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{u}$ | $c(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u}+c\mathbf{v}$ |
| associative: $(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})+\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w})$ | $(c+d)\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{u}+d\mathbf{u}$ |
| a zero $\mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{u}$ | $c(d\mathbf{u}) = (cd)\mathbf{u}$ |
| an inverse $-\mathbf{u}$ with $\mathbf{u}+(-\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}$ | $1\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}$ |

Ten axioms, and in practice you almost never check all ten. **Closure is what actually fails**,
so that is what you test first.

## Things that are vector spaces and are not arrows

The payoff is that this describes far more than $\mathbb{R}^n$:

- **$m \times n$ matrices**, added and scaled entrywise. See [[Matrix]].
- **Polynomials of degree $\leq n$.** Add two, still a polynomial of degree $\leq n$; scale one,
  same. $P_2$ has "dimension" $3$, with $\{1, x, x^2\}$ playing the role of the standard basis.
- **Continuous functions on $[a,b]$.** $(f+g)(x) = f(x)+g(x)$, $(cf)(x) = cf(x)$. This one is
  infinite-dimensional, and it is the space [[Fourier Series]] operates in: writing $f$ as a sum
  of sines and cosines is expressing a vector in terms of a [[Basis]], and
  [[Orthogonal Functions]] is the statement that this basis is orthogonal under the integral
  inner product. **That connection is the reason a first-year linear algebra course is a
  prerequisite for fourth-year analysis.**
- **Solutions to a homogeneous [[System of Linear Equations]]** $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$. Add
  two solutions, get a solution. This set is the [[Kernel and Range|kernel]] of $A$.
- **Solutions to a homogeneous linear ODE.** Same argument, and it is why the general solution
  in [[Differential Equations]] is written as $c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$: that is a linear combination in
  a two-dimensional vector space.

A non-example, to see what the axioms are doing: vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with both components
$\geq 0$ (the first quadrant). Addition is fine, but scaling by $-1$ leaves the set, so scalar
multiplication is not closed and it is not a vector space.

## Subspaces

A **subspace** is a subset of $V$ that is itself a vector space. You do not check ten axioms,
you check three:

1. $\mathbf{0} \in W$
2. closed under addition
3. closed under scalar multiplication

The rest are inherited from $V$. Geometrically, the subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^3$ are exactly:
the origin alone, every line through the origin, every plane through the origin, and
$\mathbb{R}^3$ itself. **Through the origin** is not decoration: a line that misses the origin
fails condition 1 and is not a subspace.

## Linear combinations and span

A **linear combination** of $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ is any

$$
c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k
$$

and the **span** is the set of all of them: everything you can reach from those vectors using
the only two operations you have. $\text{span}\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k\}$ is always a
subspace, and it is the smallest one containing all the $\mathbf{v}_i$.

Span in $\mathbb{R}^3$: one non-zero vector spans a line, two independent vectors span a plane,
three independent vectors span all of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Two *dependent* vectors still only span a
line, which is the whole point of [[Linear Dependence]].

A set that spans $V$ is a **spanning set**. It may be wastefully large. Trimming it down to
something with no redundancy is what produces a [[Basis]].

**This connects straight back to solving equations.** By the column reading in
[[Matrix Multiplication]], $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution exactly when $\mathbf{b}$
lies in the span of $A$'s columns. Consistency is a span question, and it always was.

## Related

- [[Linear Dependence]]: when a spanning set has redundancy in it
- [[Basis]]: a spanning set with none
- [[Kernel and Range]]: two subspaces attached to a [[Linear Transformation]]
- [[Group]] and [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]]: the same axiomatic method, one operation instead of two
- [[Sets]] in [[DISCRETE MATH]] for the underlying set notation
